extracted.intended_audience: regulatory analysts, agency decisionmakers, congressional staff, policy researchers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and recommended institutional reforms for preparing, reviewing, and correcting Regulatory Impact Analyses so that regulations address real problems, evaluate alternatives, and weigh benefits and costs accurately. Includes both substantive criteria for RIAs and procedural recommendations for ensuring compliance across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the nature and significance of the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessing the nature and significance of the problem the agency is trying to solve, so the agency knows whether there is a problem that could be solved through regulation and, if so, the agency can tailor a solution that will effectively solve it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIA should determine whether a real, significant problem exists and whether regulation is an appropriate tool. Agencies must avoid assuming a problem exists without evidence; the Report Card finds many RIAs do a poor job of this. Example anti-pattern: proposing rules without identifying the market failure or showing prior changes affected outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify a wide variety of alternative solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying a wide variety of alternative solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternatives should include non-regulatory options (e.g., enforcement of current rules, training, safety improvements, spot checks, infrastructure changes) and not be limited to narrow variations of the same approach. Example: CWPS urged consideration of stricter enforcement, training, cab safety, spot checks, and highway improvements for trucker hours rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define benefits in terms of ultimate outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining the benefits the agency seeks to achieve in terms of ultimate outcomes that affect citizens’ quality of life and assessing each alternative’s ability to achieve those outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits should be tied to final outcomes (e.g., fewer accidents, improved health) rather than intermediate measures. RIAs must analyze how each alternative changes those outcomes and quantify or qualitatively assess those effects where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and measure costs (broadly conceived)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifying the good things that regulated entities, consumers, and other stakeholders must sacrifice in order to achieve the desired outcomes under each alternative. In economics jargon, these sacrifices are known as 'costs,' but just like benefits, costs may involve far more than monetary expenditures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Costs should include compliance costs, opportunity costs, unintended harms, and non-monetary burdens. Agencies should not omit or undercount costs; CWPS and later reviews frequently found failures to estimate costs or incorrect cost estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate benefits and costs correctly and transparently
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must estimate benefits and costs rather than omit them or estimate them incorrectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical reviews (CWPS, GAO, Mercatus Report Card) show agencies often fail to estimate or misestimate benefits and costs. Good practice requires transparent methods, data sources, assumptions, and sensitivity analysis; poor practice includes failing to provide estimates or using analysis to justify a predetermined decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify market failures or reasons regulation is necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should identify whether a market failure exists that would prevent companies and individuals from internalizing the costs the regulation seeks to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: RIAs should explain why private incentives will not produce the desired outcome absent regulation. Example shortcoming: an agency failed to identify any market failure regarding driver fatigue and admitted prior hours changes had no safety effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid narrow option sets — consider fundamentally different approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternatives should not be narrow variations on the same basic approach; agencies must consider fundamentally different approaches to the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example failure: a 2010 hours-of-service RIA considered only 'no action' plus three narrow variants all reducing duty time. Good RIAs compare distinct policy levers and combinations (regulatory, enforcement, market-based, information-based).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use RIA to inform, not justify, decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis should be a tool to inform decision-making, not a means to justify predetermined decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: agencies misusing analysis to rationalize choices already made. Procedural safeguards and transparency can help ensure analysis affects decisions rather than merely supporting them after the fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply consistent analysis standards across executive and independent agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive orders requiring federal regulatory analysis do not apply to independent agencies; to better serve the public, Congress should ensure all agencies are subject to the same requirements for regulatory analysis, including review by OIRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The standard calls for parity so that independent agencies perform analyses at least as rigorous as executive-branch agencies. Scholarship finds independent agencies often conduct less thorough economic analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory requirement for RIA with judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Require Regulatory Impact Analysis by statute, with judicial review to ensure that the analysis meets minimum quality standards and that the agency adequately explained how the analysis affected its decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because agencies frequently fail to meet long-standing quality standards, a statutory mandate plus judicial oversight is recommended to enforce minimum analytic quality and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and correct nonfunctional rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonfunctional rule is a rule that does not address a current, significant problem; fails to mitigate a significant portion of the problem; or has significant unintended effects or excessive compliance costs relative to its benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should conduct retrospective review of existing rules to identify nonfunctional rules. Past retrospective efforts produced meager results; congressional action or independent review mechanisms may be necessary to prune such rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use independent, objective review mechanisms for existing regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: An expert regulatory review commission would conduct assessments of regulatory programs based on objective criteria specified in legislation, and its package of recommendations for modifying or repealing regulations would take effect unless disapproved by Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modeled on BRAC (Base Realignment and Closure Commission), this institutional reform aims to overcome agency reluctance to critically examine and eliminate nonfunctional rules by delegating review to an independent body with statutory effect.
